title: 🧢 Mdosi, chief, mkubwa…
items: People now call you boss the Nairobi way: mdosi, kiongozi, mzitu, mkubwa, chief. Tap one to see what it means — they're in flashcards and practice too.
Answer choices reshuffle every time you replay, so you can't just remember where the right one sits.
Typing is friendlier: small slips are forgiven, and alternatives like “wiki kesho” for “wiki ijayo” count.

title: ✍️ Say it your own way
items: From level 8, when you type a whole sentence, you no longer have to match our line word for word — any good Swahili that says the same thing counts.
Your sentence gets checked on the spot: you'll see what works, or exactly what to fix if it's almost right.
Full points when you use the lesson's key words; part points for other good answers.

title: 📲 Kabisa on your home screen
items: Add Kabisa to your home screen and it opens full-screen, like an app. Find it under Menu → Add to Home Screen.
Android: one tap on Install. iPhone: we show you the two taps in Safari.
Kabisa has a new logo: a Maasai shield in the colours of the flag.

title: 🤦 XP is now gonga points
items: Every lesson you complete earns you valuable gonga points.
Tap your points to see the prizes — a villa in Kiambu, a night out at Blend & Bite Bistro, and more. Redeeming works exactly as well as you'd expect.

title: 🏆 Leaderboards for every level
items: See the top 10 learners on your level, with their country flag, every time you sign in, plus where you stand.
Open it any time from the new Menu at the top right.

title: 📘 Grammar first, then the conversation
items: Every lesson now opens with “The grammar you’ll learn” — a page per structure, with the lines where you’ll use it.
Typing more than one right answer? We accept it and tell you why both work (umwambie / mwambie, naenda / ninaenda…).
The practice session is clearly your key to the next lesson — and you can exit replays you’ve already passed.
Tell us how you’d like to be addressed: women are now called mama, dada or sista. Level 10 is now Mwenyeji Mjanja.

title: 🗣️ Every word you practise, you've heard first
items: Flashcards and practice now only use words from the conversation. Where a word mattered, 27 conversations gained a line or a few words to bring it in.
Petrol station: the attendant now offers to fill the tank (kujaza) and asks “Mbele iko sawa?” before checking your oil and water.
New grammar guide: Mwambie or umwambie? Commands, polite requests and “let's” side by side, under “Read this first”.
When the English can't match the Swahili word for word, you'll see the literal meaning underneath.

title: ✌️ Two rounds from level 5
items: From level 5 each conversation has two rounds: first pick your lines, then type them. The steps at the top show where you are — round 2 is the one that counts.
Stuck on a practice line? Tap 💡 Hint to see the English.
Each person in a conversation now speaks in their own voice.

title: 🇰🇪 Everyday Kenyan, all the way up
items: Levels 7–10 now use the same everyday Kenyan agreements as the lower levels: kitu nzuri, maji mingi, mwezi iliyopita.
The standard (Sanifu) forms are still there behind the 💡 on each line.

title: 💡 One tap for notes
items: Sanifu (standard Swahili) and learner notes now sit together behind one 💡 Note — tap it on a line or a word in Key vocabulary to see both.

title: 📚 kiatu / viatu – shoe / shoes
items: Every noun in Key vocabulary and on the flashcards now shows one & many on both sides: kiatu / viatu – shoe / shoes.
Time vs. duration: saa moja is 7 a.m. (Swahili time), lisaa limoja is one hour — fixed across lessons, with a 💡 note.
More 💡 notes appear as our Kenyan editors fine-tune the lessons.

title: 🔢 One & many
items: Every noun in Key vocabulary and on the flashcards now shows its singular and plural — mwaka · miaka, kiatu · viatu.
Words Kenyans really say: taka taka, mpaka (not hadi), and more fixes from our Kenyan editors.

title: 💡 Notes on words
items: Tap a word, check a line or flip a flashcard — look for 💡 notes on other meanings and how Kenyans really use it.
In ride lessons you're now the abiria (passenger), not the mteja (customer).

title: 🔊 Real Kenyan voices + type your answers
items: Achieng and Baraka now read every line aloud — a touch slower, so you can catch every word.
From level 5 you type instead of tap: first the key word, then (from level 8) the whole line. Small typos are forgiven.

title: 📚 A bigger, friendlier course
items: 17 new lessons: home, cooking ugali, clothes at Toi, the weather, a safari, school, business and more.
Levels 1–4 now focus on everyday words — new grammar starts at level 5.
Answer choices test what words mean, not noun-class agreement.
